newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU forces Anglo to cut Lonrho stake. [CORRECTED 18:14 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EU forces Anglo to cut Lonrho stake. [CORRECTED 18:14 GMT]

text.p: In a landmark ruling on Wednesday, the European Commission forced South African mining giant Anglo American Corp to drastically cut its stake in British conglomerate Lonrho Plc to avoid controlling the platinum market.

The EU's competition watchdog said Anglo had agreed to reduce its Lonrho shareholding to 9.99 percent from 27.5 percent within an undisclosed timetable which Anglo revealed later in Johannesbourg to be two years.
Anglo expressed disappointment with the Commission ruling but said it had a number of options open.
(Corrects to delete reference to attempts to retain entire stake).
The European courts are likely to have the last word.

This is the first time the Commission has required the disposal of shares in a quoted company as a remedy to competition problems since it became the clearing house for large company linkups that affect trade in the 15-nation bloc.
It said the decision would ensure that Anglo, Lonrho and Gencor Ltd, the only other larger producer of platinum and also South African, to compete effectively against each other.
Platinum is a precious metal used mainly in exhaust car catalysts. The three companies' production sites are all in South Africa. Russia is also a big player but production is irregular.
Anglo increased its stake in Lonrho in November by acquiring 18.4 percent worth of shares from Dieter Bock, a Lonrho former chairman.

This was despite a clear warning by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert in April 1996, when the Commission also blocked the proposed merger of the platinum interests of Lonrho and Gencor.
The Commission said in a statement on Wednesday that Anglo and Lonrho would have controlled the world's platinum output.

"The companies' market shares, their low-cost reserves and the fact that the Russian producer's market position is expected to decrease in the future would lead to a combined Anglo/Lonrho having an estimated world market share for platinum production in excess of 60 percent in a few years time", it said.

The Commission said that the "most obvious solution" to the competition problems posed by such a prospect would have been for Lonrho to sell its platinum division. But it said Lonrho was unable to find a buyer other than Gencor -- a deal that the Commission could not have permitted.
The Commission left the door open for any other solution that would save Anglo from dumping its stake, although there seem to be no other options.
"This reduction is to be carried out within an agreed timetable should no other solution to the Commission's competition concerns be found," the statement said.
It said the shares in excess of 9.99 percent must be transferred to a trustee in the meantime and cannot be voted without its prior approval.
The European Court of Justice could have the final word when it rules on an appeal filed by Gencor against the 1996 decision, a move not expected for at least a year.

But the Commission's two controversial decisions are also likely to be affected by another expected court ruling on a separate case involving the takeover by German potash company Kali Salz of an east German rival.
As in the Kali Salz deal, the Commission's main argument for ruling against the platinum merger between Gencor and Lonrho was that it would create a duopoly -- in this case with Anglo American.

But a court advocate general concluded earlier this year -- when giving his opinion on the Kali Salz appeal -- that the EU's merger rules do not apply to duopolies. The court, which is expected to rule before the summer, generally follows the opinion of its advisers.
